verses.text: Cast your bread on the waters; for you shall find it after many days.
Give a portion to seven, yes, even to eight; for you don’t know what evil will be on the earth.
If the clouds are full of rain, they empty themselves on the earth; and if a tree falls toward the south, or toward the north, in the place where the tree falls, there shall it be.
He who observes the wind won’t sow; and he who regards the clouds won’t reap.
As you don’t know what is the way of the wind, nor how the bones grow in the womb of her who is with child; even so you don’t know the work of God who does all.
In the morning sow your seed, and in the evening don’t withhold your hand; for you don’t know which will prosper, whether this or that, or whether they both will be equally good.
Truly the light is sweet, and a pleasant thing it is for the eyes to see the sun.
Yes, if a man lives many years, let him rejoice in them all; but let him remember the days of darkness, for they shall be many. All that comes is vanity.

Rejoice, young man, in your youth, and let your heart cheer you in the days of your youth, and walk in the ways of your heart, and in the sight of your eyes; but know that for all these things God will bring you into judgment.
Therefore remove sorrow from your heart, and put away evil from your flesh; for youth and the dawn of life are vanity.

footnotes.content: "Casting bread on waters" was an image of generosity toward strangers and distant places—what we give, not knowing its fate, somehow returns. The Teacher knew what Jesus would later show us: that giving without expecting return is how grace moves in the world. We lose nothing when we trust it to God's hands.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: "Give to seven, even to eight"—a widening circle of generosity, because hard times come to us all, and we don't know when they'll arrive. The Teacher invites us to spread our kindness and provision as insurance, yes, but really as habit: a life shaped by openness rather than fear.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Rain falls where the clouds move it; trees fall where gravity takes them. The Teacher watches nature's honest indifference and draws out something tender—we live in a world of real limits and plain facts. Pretending otherwise wastes the time we have to act within what is true.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Watching the wind and clouds forever means never planting. The Teacher speaks here to the part of us that waits for perfect conditions, complete certainty, the signal we've been promised. But life doesn't work that way—and it never has. Some things you begin in faith, and that is enough.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: We don't know how wind moves or how a child grows in the womb—and we don't know God's work either, though He does all. The Teacher places our ignorance alongside God's knowledge not to shame us, but to quiet us. There is a kind of peace in admitting what we don't know and can't control.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Morning and evening—sow without knowing which season will bring the harvest. The Teacher tells us to act in both times, to not let doubt paralyze our hands. This is the rhythm of faithfulness: show up, do the work, let God make it grow. You don't need to know the ending.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: "Light is sweet." After so many verses on work and uncertainty, the Teacher pauses here to praise a simple thing—daylight itself, the sun on your face. In his honest catalogue of life's puzzles, he doesn't forget that brightness is a gift, and noticing it is its own kind of wisdom.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Rejoice in your many years, the Teacher says—and remember the dark days too, because they will come. He's not asking you to chase happiness at all costs, but to keep your eyes open and your heart awake, celebrating the good while it's here and carrying the weight when it comes. That's not pessimism; it's maturity.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Rejoice in your youth—follow your heart and your eyes—but know God will bring you into judgment. The Teacher isn't denying joy or locking it away behind rules; he's inviting you to enjoy it with your eyes open. We live under both gift and consequence, and both are true, and both matter.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Readers today hear an echo here: youth and its bright beginnings pass like morning. The Teacher invites us to strip away what won't matter later—the spite, the petty flesh-complaints—not out of severity, but because we know now, even then, that they cost us the sweetness of the days we're given. Looking back, we're grateful when we lived lighter.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight
